title: ‘Don’t pick winners’: Future Fund reveals blueprint for AI investing
full_text:
The Future Fund believes it is still too early to pick winners from AI, instead the $330bn manager is spreading its bets across the entire tech value chain, from chipmakers, data centres to software, and even by country.
Chief executive Raphael Arndt told The Australian AI represents one of the biggest thematic shifts for global markets in generations, but cautions that just like the dot.com era, there is plenty of scope for today’s AI heroes to be disrupted in coming years. This is why it is prudent at this time to build defence in its portfolio, rather than chase high-conviction bets.
“We can’t pick it; it’s too uncertain, too volatile,” Dr Arndt said in an interview. “What we need to do is think really carefully about all the different options and where we might have AI exposure through the portfolio.”
Investments across the fund need to be managed so they are “not too big, or too small, but also so they’re very widely spread”.
“The probability of accurately picking the company, country or technology stack that will dominate is exceptionally low.”
His comments represent an important departure in how major investors are chasing returns in AI, with current bets on just a handful of big names representing one of the most historically crowded trades on Wall Street.
The Canberra-backed fund has issued a major position paper around adding resilience in its portfolio in the era of AI. This builds on the four major themes the Future Fund highlighted in its 2021 paper, The New Investment Order, where it identified the recurring features of modern markets. These included: increasing volatility; more populism and government interventions; greater inflation and supply shocks; and geopolitics would have a bigger impact on markets.
Dr Arndt acknowledges the pace of AI development has exceeded even the Future Fund’s own expectations and its own value and quality investment tilt. This meant the fund had an underweight position heading into the current boom, particularly around hyperscalers and some data centre operators. While it has $2.1bn exposure to the likes of Nvidia and $2bn to Google’s Alphabet, this compares to some of Australia’s big industry super funds such as AustralianSuper, UniSuper and HESTA, which have significant direct exposure to the AI trade as a proportion of assets.
Future Fund AI strategy
Despite its early caution, the Future Fund believes AI represents a “profound opportunity”, with large upside potential.
This comes from a belief that AI is likely to be major driver of economic growth and therefore tailwinds for investment returns over the long term. Meanwhile the gap between AI leaders and laggards will create opportunities for active investors.
Dr Arndt says his fund needs to “update its thinking” but as an ultra long-term investor it needs to consider the broader implications spanning economics, politics and business.
AI is “too important to ignore or be passive about it”, Dr Arndt said. “It will drive how economies evolve, infrastructure develops. It will have a national security lens over it, and ultimately most businesses will rely on it in some way.”
His comments come as tech-heavy Nasdaq and Wall Street benchmark the S&P 500 are tracking near record highs, propelled by AI-linked names including chipmaker Nvidia and a host of cloud providers from Amazon, Microsoft and Google-parent Alphabet. Still, there remain ongoing doubts the hundreds of billions in AI infrastructure spending by major tech names will translate into profitable revenue.
Mega floats, market froth, and whether investing in SpaceX risky or smart
In its paper, the Future Fund has structured its direct AI exposure across four layers.
These are hardware players such as Nvidia; infrastructure like data centres and power grid; platforms such as Microsoft, Google and the unlisted Open AI; finally foundation models sitting in funders of private equity and venture capital.
Beyond direct exposure there’s also implications for the Future Fund’s other investments, with the AI build out already driving inflation in parts, there’s a shift in some commodity pricing while longer term it may prove to be deflationary by improving productivity and reducing costs. AI technology may also have major implications for monetary policy.
Even with the note of caution in the position paper, Dr Arndt stopped short of calling current AI valuations a “bubble” given there is genuine revenue and margin growth behind some names.
But he has flagged real risks if that growth proves unsustainable, alongside emerging constraints like chip shortages, skilled labour, planning permissions, and community pushback on power demands that all could hit valuations.
“It’s hard to call it a bubble because of the earnings growth. But it may it may emerge as a bubble – we have to be careful about that,” he said.
While today’s incumbents like Nvidia, Alphabet and even AI model developers such as Anthropic or OpenAI seem unassailable with first-mover advantages, they risk being disrupted entirely by new entrants.
Over the longer term the technology becomes so widespread and mature that it stops being the edge to individual names and instead lifts the whole market.
Even if there is a crash or sorts, Dr Arndt points out that just like the dot.com boom, the underlying technology and infrastructure will endure.
Dr Arndt also cautioned that the staggering amount of capex directed into AI infrastructure, including the near $US800bn ($1.1 trillion) commitments by the hyperscalers this year alone and rising to $US1 trillion in coming years risks “slowing investment in other things”. This is already starting to be seen with the rising cost of debt.
There is also the potential to destabilise job markets. The Fund notes that “responsible AI” has rapidly evolved beyond merely having a “human in the loop”, and that social expectations around AI governance will continue to shift. The social-licence pressure is emerging as the biggest risk for AI development.
The paper also gives a nod to Australia through the Albanese government’s “balanced” approached through its recent AI statement that outlined an intent to embrace the technology while protecting intellectual property and setting minimum standards for data centres around energy and water use.
In terms of “sovereignisation” of AI, the US is currently leading the race in foundation large language models through Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, while China is determined to develop its own rivals with Moonshot AI and Alibaba. Other parts of Asia such as Japan, Taiwan and Korea are emerging as supply chain leaders. Europe is taking a more cautious approach that could have implications for valuations, the Future Fund said.
“Countries that fall behind will face more than slower growth,” Dr Arndt says. “Weak domestic AI capability risks diminished industrial competitiveness, reduced strategic autonomy and growing dependence on external providers for critical systems including areas like healthcare, defence and financial services.”
This dependence “becomes a geopolitical vulnerability”, he said.
